content: Obeticholic acid is indicated for the treatment of primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) in adults without cirrhosis or with compensated cirrhosis who do not exhibit evidence of portal hypertension. It can be used in combination with ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) in patients who have had an inadequate response to UDCA for at least one year or as monotherapy in patients who are intolerant to UDCA. The safety and efficacy of obeticholic acid have not been established in all populations. While no overall differences in safety or effectiveness were observed in patients older than 65 years, increased sensitivity in some older individuals cannot be ruled out. Cholestyramine, colesevelam, and colestipol can decrease the levels or effects of obeticholic acid by binding to the drug in the gastrointestinal tract. To mitigate this interaction, obeticholic acid should be administered at least 4 hours before or 4 hours after taking bile acid-binding resins. Therapy should be modified or closely monitored in such cases. Obeticholic acid can increase the levels or effects of theophylline and tizanidine by affecting hepatic enzyme CYP1A2 metabolism. CYP1A2 substrates with a narrow therapeutic index should be closely monitored, and their doses adjusted accordingly. Therapy should be modified or closely monitored in these situations. Common adverse effects of obeticholic acid include pruritus (56-70%), fatigue (19-25%), severe pruritus (19-23%), reduced HDL-C (9-20%), abdominal pain and discomfort (10-19%), rash (7-10%), arthralgia (6-10%), oropharyngeal pain (7-8%), dizziness (7%), constipation (7%), peripheral edema (3-7%), palpitations (3-7%), pyrexia (7%), thyroid function abnormalities (4-6%), and eczema (3-6%). Hepatobiliary disorders such as liver failure, new-onset cirrhosis, increased direct and total bilirubin, and new or worsening jaundice have been reported. Patients with complete biliary obstruction, decompensated cirrhosis (e.g., Child-Pugh Class B or C), or a prior decompensation event, as well as those with compensated cirrhosis with evidence of portal hypertension (e.g., ascites, gastroesophageal varices, persistent thrombocytopenia), should be carefully evaluated before initiating therapy. Patients with PBC often exhibit hyperlipidemia characterized by elevated total cholesterol, primarily due to increased HDL-C levels. Monitoring for reductions in HDL-C is recommended. For patients who do not respond after one year at the highest recommended tolerable dosage (10 mg/day) and experience a reduction in HDL-C, the potential risks and benefits of continuing treatment should be weighed. Severe pruritus has been reported in some patients. For those with new-onset or worsening pruritus, consider treatment with bile acid-binding resins, antihistamines, dose reduction, or temporary dose interruption. There is limited human data on the use of obeticholic acid during pregnancy, and the available information is insufficient to determine drug-associated risks. There is no information on the presence of obeticholic acid in human milk, its effects on breastfed infants, or its effects on milk production. When considering the use of obeticholic acid in breastfeeding mothers, weigh the developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding against the mother’s clinical need for the drug and any potential adverse effects on the breastfed infant from the drug or the underlying maternal condition. Obeticholic acid is a farnesoid X receptor (FXR) agonist. FXR is a nuclear receptor expressed in the liver, intestine, kidney, and adipose tissue that regulates genes involved in bile acid synthesis and transport, lipid metabolism, and glucose homeostasis. Activation of FXR suppresses de novo bile acid synthesis in hepatocytes and increases bile acid transport out of hepatocytes, thereby reducing hepatocyte exposure to bile acids. Obeticholic acid is highly protein-bound (>99%) and has a volume of distribution of 618 L. It is conjugated with glycine or taurine in the liver and secreted into bile. These conjugates are either reabsorbed in the small intestine for enterohepatic recirculation or excreted in feces. Approximately 87% of the drug is excreted in feces, with less than 3% excreted in urine. Obeticholic acid can be taken with or without food. When co-administering obeticholic acid with bile acid-binding resins, separate the doses by at least 4 hours before or after the resin, or as great an interval as possible. Store obeticholic acid at 20-25°C (68-77°F), with excursions permitted to 15-30°C (59-86°F).
